Count SemiPrimes With an Optional Partial-Sieve Cutoff

semiPrimeCount.Rd

Count positive integers less than or equal to \(n\) with exactly two prime factors, counted with multiplicity, excluding the first \(a\) primes as factors. This is the correction term \(P_2(n, a)\) used in Meissel and Lehmer prime counting.

Usage

semiPrimeCount(n, a = 0, nThreads = NULL)

Arguments

n

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\).

a

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\). This is the number of initial primes excluded as factors, not a prime value. The default, a = 0, permits every prime. For example, a = 1 excludes the prime 2, so only odd semiprimes are counted.

nThreads

Requested number of threads. The default is NULL for serial execution. Requests are capped by the available hardware and the useful work in the calculation. Small or simple cases may use fewer threads. This argument is validated even when the result is immediate.

Details

Logical inputs FALSE and TRUE are converted to 0 and 1, respectively. The thread count must be positive, so nThreads = FALSE is not supported.

Mathematical definition

Let \(p_i\) denote the \(i\)th prime. The function counts products \(p_i p_j \le n\) with \(a < i \le j\). The ordering counts each integer once: \(2 \cdot 3\) and \(3 \cdot 2\) do not give two different semiprimes. Equal factors are allowed, so prime squares such as 4, 9, and 25 are included when their prime factor is permitted.

When \(a = 0\), the excluded set is empty; no zeroth prime is needed. The ten semiprimes at most 30 are 4, 6, 9, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, 25, 26. Excluding the first prime leaves 9, 15, 21, 25, so semiPrimeCount(30, 1) is 4.

Write \(\pi(t)\) for the number of primes at most \(t\), and set \(b = \pi(\lfloor \sqrt n \rfloor)\). For a fixed smaller factor \(p_i\), the larger factor has an index from \(i\) through \(\pi(\lfloor n / p_i \rfloor)\). Consequently, $$P_2(n, a) = \sum_{i=a+1}^{b} \left[\pi(\lfloor n / p_i \rfloor) - i + 1\right].$$ A sum with no terms is zero. In particular, the answer is zero for \(n < 4\) or \(a \ge b\). Equivalently, the smallest permitted prime square must be at most \(n\) for any semiprime to qualify.

Relation to prime counting

For Meissel's cutoff \(a = \pi(\lfloor n^{1/3} \rfloor)\), the partial sieve leaves 1, the primes beyond the cutoff, and qualifying semiprimes. Thus, for \(n \ge 1\), $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1 - P_2(n, a).$$ The function primePhi supplies \(\Phi(n, a)\). Lehmer's smaller cutoff also requires triPrimeCount; see primeCount for the full formula.

Note

The calculation prepares prime and prime-count tables with storage proportional to \(\sqrt n\). Larger prime-count queries in the sum use the shared partial-sieve evaluator or a segmented sieve, selected according to the input, cutoff, and useful thread budget. The segmented sieve uses bounded buffers for each worker; the function does not allocate a dense table through \(n / p_{a+1}\).

At the largest supported \(n\), the square-root table has limit 94,906,265. Its dense prime-count entries alone require \(4(L + 1)\) bytes for limit \(L\), about 362 MiB at the maximum, excluding prime vectors, the shared Phi cache, temporary storage, and allocation overhead. Workers within one call share the prepared tables; separate calls prepare their own tables. A valid numeric input may still require substantial time or memory.

Value

A single whole number giving \(P_2(n, a)\). The result has type integer when it is at most .Machine$integer.max, and type double otherwise. The count is exact throughout the supported range.

Author

Joseph Wood

See also

primePhi, triPrimeCount, primeCount, primeSieve

Examples

## Count all semiprimes, then exclude 2 as a factor
semiPrimeCount(30)    ## 10
#> [1] 10
semiPrimeCount(30, 1) ## 4
#> [1] 4

## Equal prime factors are included
semiPrimeCount(4)     ## 1, from 2 * 2
#> [1] 1
semiPrimeCount(3)     ## 0
#> [1] 0
semiPrimeCount(0)     ## 0
#> [1] 0
semiPrimeCount(30, 100) ## 0
#> [1] 0

## A modest calculation with a requested thread budget
semiPrimeCount(10^6, nThreads = 2)
#> [1] 210035
